Bellfield Design recently asked its staff how they felt about their hybrid work schedule. Out of 84 employees invited to take the internal survey, 56 sent back answers. From that group, 39 people said they could concentrate on their tasks more easily when they worked from home. This suggests that working remotely might help some employees focus, but it does not prove that productivity has gone up for the whole company.

The survey also pointed out problems with how people talk to each other. A few respondents said it was harder to set up casual chats when their coworkers were in different places. Other people said that planned online meetings helped them keep up with decisions made about projects. The survey did not ask employees if the quality of their work was better, worse, or the same at home compared to the office.

Managers will keep the current schedule for three more months while they gather more feedback. People can still choose whether or not they want to take part in the next survey. Since these results come from what employees reported themselves and leave out the people who didn't answer, should the data be viewed with caution? More evidence is needed before anyone can conclude how hybrid working affects overall performance.
